name: Letrozole

lead: Letrozole is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal breast cancer, also used in fertility treatment. Looksmax.org users, including teenagers, discuss it for delaying growth-plate closure to add height.
No controlled trial in healthy adolescents was found; forum users themselves warn it is the strongest option and can crash oestrogen.

paras: It blocks the aromatase enzyme, lowering conversion of androgens to oestrogen. Since oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, the hope is a longer growth window.
The label lists bone density loss, raised cholesterol, fatigue and dizziness, hot flashes and joint pain, and it can cause fetal harm. Prescription-only; height use is off-label.

lead: Letrozole is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor taken by mouth. The US label lists adjuvant and extended adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer in postmenopausal women, and first- and second-line treatment of advanced disease.[1] It is also widely used in fertility medicine for ovulation induction.[2][3]

On looksmax.org it is discussed mainly for heightmaxxing, by users who hope to delay growth-plate closure by lowering oestrogen, often together with growth hormone or MK-677, and some of whom describe themselves as 15 or 16 years old.[4][5][6] Users compare it with anastrozole and exemestane, and several describe it as the most potent and the most likely to crash oestrogen.[5] No controlled trial in healthy adolescents testing letrozole for adult height was found in the sources reviewed.
The label warns of decreased bone mineral density, increased cholesterol, fatigue and dizziness, and embryo-fetal toxicity; it is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1] It is a prescription medicine.
infobox: Breast cancer in postmenopausal women (US label)

paras: Breast cancer indications on the US label are described above.[1] Letrozole has been compared with tamoxifen in early breast cancer and used after five years of tamoxifen in randomised trials, and combined with CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib and ribociclib in advanced and early disease.[7][8][9][10] In reproductive medicine, a Cochrane review of aromatase inhibitors for ovulation induction in polycystic ovary syndrome, a mini-review of its use in female infertility and a meta-analysis in unexplained infertility examine letrozole, which was introduced for ovulation induction around 2001.[2][11][12]

Appearance-related interest centres on height. A looksmax.org poster says a few trials of aromatase inhibitors in short stature suggest letrozole may be more effective than exemestane, while adding that it can crash oestrogen and that too little oestrogen can cause brittle bones and stunted growth.[5] Other threads ask which inhibitor is best for height, or where to obtain letrozole with MK-677.[4][6][13][14]

The US label lists decreases in bone mineral density, increases in cholesterol, and fatigue, dizziness and somnolence as warnings. Its most common adverse reactions (over 20%) include hot flashes, arthralgia, flushing, asthenia, oedema, headache, dizziness, hypercholesterolaemia, increased sweating, bone pain and musculoskeletal symptoms.[1] The label states letrozole can cause fetal harm and is contraindicated in pregnancy, with postmarketing reports of spontaneous abortions and congenital defects.[1]
Forum users also report concern: one reply to a height thread says exemestane is safer and harder to crash oestrogen with, whereas letrozole will destroy you.[5]

Letrozole inhibits the aromatase enzyme, which converts androgens to oestrogens, reducing oestrogen synthesis; this is the principal source of oestrogen in postmenopausal women.[1][2] A review of letrozole's pharmacology and clinical profile is available.[15]

Human trials are overwhelmingly in breast cancer and infertility. Examples include the comparison of letrozole and tamoxifen, MONALEESA and PALOMA combination trials, and large adjuvant trials.[7][8][9][10][16] Registered trials include a 2018 trial of letrozole in stimulated IVF cycles (n=900).[17]
No published trial of letrozole for increasing height in healthy adolescents was identified in the sources reviewed; the claims above come from forum discussion.

Many threads are started by teenagers asking about letrozole for height, often combined with growth hormone or MK-677, some asking how to buy it without parental knowledge.[4][6][13] Responses range from encouragement, to the suggestion of alternatives such as endoxifen, to dismissive remarks about risking health for small height gains.[18] One thread title attributes a dramatic change in attitudes to women to letrozole use, reflecting anecdotal accounts of mood and hormone effects.[19] On T Nation, a user planning a testosterone cycle discusses using letrozole powder as an aromatase inhibitor and the difficulty of measuring small quantities.[20]

lore.intro: Letrozole is discussed as the strongest of the aromatase inhibitors for height, with frequent warnings from other users about crashing oestrogen.[5][4]
